verdict: OK to lend in Halol two-wheelers — pursue Tier-1/Tier-2 OEM-linked component and EV-conversion suppliers with tight monthly discipline; avoid single-OEM-dependent assemblers and thin-margin dealers.
title: Halol two-wheelers: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Halol is a vehicle-assembly town, and the two-wheeler money here sits in the component and sub-assembly shops feeding assembly lines, not in the brand owners. **A parts maker buys steel, aluminium, plastics and electronics, converts them on presses and moulds, and sells just-in-time to an OEM.** Cash comes back fast when the buyer is a large OEM and slow when it is the aftermarket or export channel [10]. So when a proposal lands, check who the top buyer is and what share of revenue it carries; if one OEM is above roughly half, ask for the supply agreement and payment terms in writing.

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in tooling, process yield and the OEM relationship; cash sits in receivables and inventory.** OEM-linked suppliers run smaller working-capital needs because OEMs pay promptly on just-in-time terms, while aftermarket and export sellers carry longer cycles [10]. Pricing power is thin — ICRA notes high competitive intensity forces high operational discipline [8]. So when a proposal lands, check receivable days against the stated OEM terms; if receivables are stretching beyond terms, ask whether the buyer mix has shifted to aftermarket.

## What has changed now
**Demand is strong and credit is running ahead of output.** India-wide two-wheeler output rose 25.3% YoY and 22.7% Apr-to-date [D], while bank credit to the sector grew 27.0% against that 22.7% output — a 4.3 pp gap [D]. Gujarat GST collections are up 11.9% Apr-to-date versus India's 6.1% [D], a genuine local tailwind. Peer results confirm the volume: Bajaj, TVS and Hero all posted strong Q2 with industry sales up 27% [4], and Bajaj called Q2 a record with its EV business now margin-accretive domestically [5]. But Hero shows the other side — margin pressure despite strong growth, with input-cost inflation and competitive pressure cited [6][7]. **Volume is not the risk; margin and the credit-output gap are.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue Tier-1 and Tier-2 component suppliers with diversified OEM books, and EV-conversion and scooter-part makers riding the premium/EV shift [7].** Avoid assemblers or dealers whose entire order book is one OEM, and avoid aftermarket-only sellers with long receivable cycles [10]. Structure against the working-capital cycle: cash-flow-based limits, receivables-backed drawing power, and a covenant that margin stays above the level at which cash accrual holds [11]. Take monthly stock-and-receivables statements, quarterly GST returns, and a monthly buyer-mix report. Note the rating sources [8][9][10][11] are undated methodology papers — treat them as principles, not current numbers.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch receivable days, buyer concentration and margin together, not separately.** A fall in operating margin that cuts cash accrual by 30% is an explicit downgrade trigger in rating criteria [11]. If receivables stretch while the top-buyer share rises, ask for the OEM's payment confirmation. If monthly GST turnover drops below the trailing quarter average, reprice or reduce the limit. Halol-specific local reporting is thin — sources [1][2][3] carry little usable financial detail — so lean on first principles and the peer set above.
watch: Monthly GST returns vs trailing quarter average (monthly)
Turnover falls below trailing-quarter average -> ask for order book and reprice limit
Receivable days vs stated OEM terms (monthly)
Receivables stretch beyond terms -> ask for buyer-mix shift and OEM payment confirmation
Single OEM above half of revenue -> require supply agreement and cap exposure
Cash accrual falls 30% -> downgrade internal grade and reduce limit [11]
Credit growth stays above output growth -> tighten new sanctions to diversified buyers [D]

news_why: Strong output and peer Q2 growth offset by margin pressure and credit running ahead of output.
